utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. Two people on their feet. Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour, and thank you to Mr. Saxon for giving me precedence. Simply to indicate that I would wish to excuse Ms. Residovic, who will be here later this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mettraux, for that courtesy, but you don't need to repeat it just for occasional absences. We fully understand. And good morning to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm sorry you waited yesterday and then had to be disappointed, but we had reached nearly the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's perfectly all right, sir. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: May I remind you of the affirmation which I think is still sufficiently in your memory. It still applies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bezruchenko, if you could turn, please, to what is the document at tab 26 of your binder. This is 65 ter number 969.2. It was a document which the Prosecution received from the Archive of the Military Intelligence Department of the Ministry of Defence of Macedonia. And, Your Honours, this document is referenced at footnotes 106, 116, 122, 285, 286, 288 and 289 in Mr. Bezruchenko's amended expert report. Do you recognise this document, Mr. Bezruchenko?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And just, in general terms, what does this document deal with?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally speaking, this document deals with various aspects related to the National Liberation Army. It deals with the organisation, structure, logistics, strategy, tactics, financial support and other issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Can we turn, please, to page 3 of this document. It's also page 3 in the Macedonian version. Mr. Bezruchenko, what does this page of the document tell us?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: This page presents an organisational diagram of the NLA. At the top of this page, you see the box indicating the NLA Command Staff, and below this box you see two boxes indicating the western and eastern fronts, and you also see, at the bottom of the page, six boxes indicating six NLA brigades; namely, 111th, 112th, 113th, 115th, 116th.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And at the top, there's a box that says: "NLA chief of Staff, General Major Gzim Ostreni." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The significance of the fact -- What is the significance, if any, of the fact that the six brigades are mentioned here?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my assessment, the significance of this fact is many-fold. First of all, it means that the NLA had the Military Staff, General Staff, which was at the top of the military hierarchy and in charge of planning military operations on the ground, which is the most essential function of any military organisation. And the NLA also had combat units on the ground of the brigade size, which is six units in various parts of the country; namely, in eastern and western front.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Can we turn, please, to page -- excuse me, paragraph 42 of Mr. Bezruchenko's amended report, please. This is Part 2.2.2 of Mr. Bezruchenko's report, dealing -- and this part deals with the NLA. Do you see paragraph 42, Mr. Bezruchenko?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Just very briefly, what are the important facts that you describe in paragraph 42?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Paragraph 42 is based on various sources which are the international sources, namely, NATO sources, Macedonian military sources, as well as the NLA sources, and there is general agreement relating to all these sources, general concurrence, that the NLA had six brigades on the ground and had its headquarters which was located in Prizren sometime, then in Djakovica, and they also had headquarters in various locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If you can turn your mind a little further down the page, please, at what is paragraph 45. The salient facts that you describe in this paragraph are what?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: This paragraph describes various sources and assessments related to the NLA personnel strengths. For example, the document which is cited under footnote 40 estimates the initial strengths of the NLA at 2.400 men, or another source, which is the source made by prominent Macedonian military experts in their book which was released after the conflict, estimates the strengths of the NLA up to 8.000 men. It's really difficult to make a precise estimate of what was the actual fighting force on the NLA at the last stage of the conflict, but I think the figure of 8.000 is not too far from reality.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. If we can return to what is tab 26, please, what we were looking at a moment ago, 65 ter 969.2, and if we can look at what is page 4 in the English version, also page 4 in the Macedonian version. We see here, in paragraph 6 at the top of page 4, we see a list of -- it appears to be weaponry. Can you describe what this document is telling us here?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe this document was released sometime around the date of 26 September 2001, which was the date of closing the NATO Operation Essential Harvest dealing with collection of NLA weapons. This document deals with assessments of various arms and weaponry in possession of the NLA. While just skimming through the document, you can easily assess the amount of the weaponry in NLA's disposal. For example, automatic rifles of Yugoslav, Chinese and Bulgarian origin, 12.000 pieces; semi-automatic rifles, 2.000 pieces; sniper rifles, 800 pieces; light machine-guns, 300 pieces; pistols, 12.000 pieces, and so on and so on and so on. Well, of particular significance on this list, in fact, are some weapons which could contribute significantly into the NLA war effort. These are, for example: Anti-aircraft missiles, Srela-2 missiles apparently in the inventory of up to 150 pieces; Stinger, American-made missiles of similar type. Well, in fact, pretty close in its design to Strela-2M, around 20 pieces; antitank missiles, around 90 pieces. Multi-barrelled grenade launchers, 1500 pieces; recoilless cannons, 80 pieces. So this is a pretty impressive list. At the bottom of this page, you also see the figures which represent the amount of weapons collected by NATO forces in Macedonia throughout the operation dubbed Essential Harvest.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That was after the Ohrid Agreement?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was after the Ohrid Agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do we see a discrepancy?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we definitely see a discrepancy here. A very superficial analysis of this document would suggest that only a small fraction of the weapons had been collected.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we can turn to what is page 13 in this -- in the English version of this document. And it's page 12 in the Macedonian version, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bezruchenko, do you want to turn to page 13 in the English?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm just watching it on the screen, but let me do it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It has the words: "Training of members of the so-called NLA" at the top.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It's the 13th page in the English version.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry. Just one sec, please. I'm still watching for the document on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you see it on the screen, Mr. Bezruchenko? Could you work that way?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What was, if any, the significance of the information on this page underneath the heading: "Training of members of the so-called NLA"; what do we see here?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this page describes locations of various training centres which apparently were during the military training for the NLA, and we have numerous locations here. Well, in Kosovo for a while, in the Republic of Albania, as well as locations in Macedonia proper, probably about two or three dozen of such locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And why would the existence of these training centres be significant for the purposes of your work?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The training of military personnel is one of the factors which contributes to the combat efficiency of any military force. It's probably one of the most important factors, anyway, which would suggest to me that if such training centres did exist, the NLA had an institutional, established capabilities of establishing, running and administering such centres, as well as producing sufficiently-trained fighters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we turn, please, to what is page 18 in the English version, and it would be page 16 in the Macedonian version. It's a paragraph starting at the top. You might be able to see it on the screen,

utterances.speaker: MR. BEZRUCHENKO
utterances.text: "The terrorist activities were carried out on a principle of connected vessels, that is, by transferring the focus from one to another crisis region and by constantly maintaining tension in the entire crisis territory."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Are you with me?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Why, from a military -- from a military perspective, what do you take from that description of the NLA activity?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is the classic military strategy, if you wish, which is aimed at extending the adversary's forces over a wider area to make sure that the adversary does not really concentrate his forces at one decisive point to deliver a decisive blow or strike. It also makes it difficult for the adversary to exercise manoeuvre of the forces and shift the reinforcements and supplies from front to front. Essentially, this is a classical strategy to put an adversary into a disadvantageous position.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bezruchenko, I believe it was last week when you were testifying. At page 6058 of the transcript, you provided a military definition of the term "armed conflict," and as part of your definition, you said the following. You said: "A conflict is normally of protracted nature. It involves use of arms and weaponry and is normally waged for attainment of certain military or political goals." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we could turn, Your Honours, please, to what is paragraph 150 of Mr. Bezruchenko's amended expert report. For those following in English, it's on page 41.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you see paragraph 150?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm wondering whether -- if you could just focus on the first sentence or so of that paragraph and explain to us, in general terms, what the NLA's strategy was and aim during 2001.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Your Honours, I would just read this paragraph out loud. I mean, I will read just the first sentence out loud: "Analysis of the NLA's strategy indicates that the aim was to hold and expand the territory under its control, stretching the government's forces to the limit, thus denying the government the opportunity to exercise any authority in the NLA-controlled areas." In fact, my assessment is that the NLA's strategy was indeed aimed at expanding the territorial control of certain areas in Macedonia and dislodge the government forces from those areas, exercising their own authority there. Its strategy was also to deny the entry of the government forces in these areas and any attempt of the government forces to recapture those areas were invariably met with armed resistance, which resulted in casualties for the Macedonian security forces. As the reports in the media were hitting the front pages of Macedonian and international newspapers, well, the pressure on the government to do something about the crisis and this war was mounting. Well, this is what exactly was happening, and the NLA's political goals were partly based on attracting the attention of the International Community to the crisis in Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bezruchenko, could you turn your mind, please, to the very next paragraph. It's paragraph 151. Because you just brought us to that, I wanted to ask you: Were the NLA's military objectives, according to your assessment, directed towards a central political goal?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, they were. The paragraph 151 describes the military objectives that the NLA had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Take a look at the very first sentence of paragraph 151, if I may.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Focus your attention. What was the central goal?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The central goal was to accept the terms of settlement of the conflict on the NLA terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Who would accept that -- the terms of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, those political parties which signed the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You're referring -- well, can you take a look at what the first sentence says, Mr. Bezruchenko?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It says --

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The NLA?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: "To force the government to accept NLA terms of settlement of the conflict."

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. And what were they, were they, what you referred to as the consecutive military objectives of the NLA, what were they?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my assessment, there were a number of objectives that the NLA had, and of course they could not really be realised simultaneously in one go. The initial objective was to establish a basis for operations in remote mountain areas on the border with Kosovo, namely, Skopska Crna Gora and Sar mountains. The military geography of the area offered advantages to the NLA. It was difficult for the government forces to access --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Bezruchenko.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Sorry to intervene, Your Honour, but the witness appears to be reading simply from the report. I'm not sure if it's of any use in that case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If it's from the report, it would not seem to be directly objectionable, but I leave it to Mr. Saxon to decide whether it is the most practical way he wants to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bezruchenko, just very briefly, can you describe what the military objectives of the NLA were?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Very briefly, the initial objective was to establish a sufficient base for operations on the ground. It was only logical to assume that such base naturally could exist in the remote mountain areas on the border with Kosovo and Albania, which would provide easy access for supplies of weapons, ammunition and personnel across the border. The second objective was to concentrate military activities in two key areas, again, not too far away from the border. Those were Tetovo and Lipkovo. The next objective was to expand gradually the territory of control around these two areas, pushing down south from Tetovo, south and southwest, and from Lipkovo, southeast. Another one was to expand these territorial gains to such a degree that it would make it very difficult for the Macedonian government and authorities to exercise control in these areas and to move their forces sufficiently, in an efficient way, to defeat the NLA. And finally, in the course of the conflict, inevitably there would come a point where this territorial control, coupled with the NLA activities and mounting casualties, would force the government to accept the terms of political settlement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you. And just to clarify, you mentioned Lipkovo. Is Lipkovo in the same general area as Kumanovo?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we can go back to what is tab 26 in your binder, 65 ter number 969.2, but this time to page 18 -- again page 18 in the English version, page 17 in the Macedonian version. It's the same page where we were before, Mr. Bezruchenko.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You see, towards the bottom of the page, there is a subtitle called: "The NLA's Strategy." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And that tells us to take over control -- first of all, "to attract and to maintain international attention and intervention," and,"to take over control of the undefended territory and protection of the same with minimum losses (to avoid close combat), to force the government of the Republic of Macedonia to negotiate." And you see that phrase in parentheses, "Close combat"?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Why was that part of the NLA strategy?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was the expression of the classical doctrine of asymmetrical warfare which was employed by the NLA. Well, it is only obvious that in direct combat, the NLA would certainly suffer from the disadvantages which it had, which were represented by the advantages of the Macedonian regular forces which were better armed and better equipped.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. If we can turn now to the very next page, please, still on page 17 in the Macedonian version.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: In the middle of the page, there is a paragraph that begins with: "For a coordinated presentation ..." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And that paragraph says: "For a coordinated presentation of the Albanian political subjects in the Republic of Macedonia at the forthcoming negotiations, in the course of July, in Prizren a meeting was held between Ali Ahmeti on one side and leaders of the largest Albanian political parties in the Republic of Macedonia, Arben Xhaferi, Imer Imeri, when they signed a declaration that they support the political demands of the so-called NLA." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: This declaration, did it become known by a particular name?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What was that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Prizren Platform.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you just speak up a little bit, please?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Prizren Platform.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. And why was the signing of this Prizren Platform significant for you, if it was?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: One should be remind that the DPA and PDP, the two biggest ethnic Albanian political parties, were parliamentary parties in Macedonia with legally-elected representatives in the Macedonian Assembly. The significance of the fact that this declaration was signed by representatives of these political parties and the NLA was that, in fact, the political parties, these political parties, supported the political goals of the NLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Your Honours, at this time I would seek to tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, we won't object to the actual tendering of the document, but there may be issues that are relevant to weight and also to the line of questioning of the Defence, and those matters would be first: The Prosecution has indicated, I believe, that the document comes from the Archives of the Military Intelligence Service in Macedonia, but we would be grateful if Mr. Saxon could indicate whether he knows it, who prepared this document, on the basis of what information, and also, Your Honour, the date, if any, at which this document was prepared.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution does not know who prepared this document. There is no indication on the document. It does not know on what basis it was prepared, although if you allow me, I might be able to help us by asking Mr. Bezruchenko a few questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bezruchenko, when you read this document, given your military experience, do you have at least an assessment or a sense of who it would have been prepared and from what kind of information?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would imagine that this document was prepared by the analytical section or department within the Macedonian Military Intelligence, which is G2 of the Macedonian General Staff, and the document was prepared on the basis of analysis of available information which had been collected by the Macedonian Military Intelligence throughout the conflict. I believe the document was apparently prepared and released sometime in September 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution -- obviously, this document does not have a date on it. However, the English translation indicates that most of the time the English translation is written in the past tense, so that would seem to indicate that this document would have been prepared at least sometime after the Ohrid Agreement. And since Operation Essential Harvest was well underway, that would be another indication that perhaps as early as September of 2001, this document could have been created.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The document will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P485, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bezruchenko, if you could turn, please, to paragraph 95 in your amended expert report, please. Your Honours, this is on page 24 of the English version. And this part of the amended expert report is part 2.5. It's entitled: "NLA command and control."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Are you with me, Mr. Bezruchenko?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: There's a summary there. You don't need to read it all, but can you just briefly describe your assessment of the NLA's command-and-control system, please?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, the NLA can't really be equated with sophisticated, modern armies, but there are numerous examples which essentially would suggest that in this world, there are lots of various armies and groups which are fighting with some degree of efficient control. Well, my assessment is that the NLA had basic elements of the command-and-control system. It had the political leadership, it had the General Staff, and it had the combat units on the ground which were implementing the orders of the political leadership and General Staff. It also had basic command procedures.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It did have a functioning chain of command?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did. If it had the political leadership and if it had the General Staff and if it had the brigades on the ground, it definitely had the line of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And could you describe the military hierarchy of the NLA? You discussed this briefly in paragraph 96.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I mentioned at the very top of the NLA was the political leadership, Ali Ahmeti and his immediate staff. On the level immediately below him was the NLA General Staff or Military Staff as it is referred in some documents. This Staff was headed by Major General Gzim Ostreni. There was an intermediate link as well of two original commands, the Kumanovo Command and the Tetovo Command, and finally there were six brigades on the ground. In short, it was a vertical hierarchy which was functioning from top to bottom as in any other military organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: In paragraph 96, you refer to the principle of unity of military and political control. Can you briefly describe what this principle of unity means, in a military sense?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in a way, this principle can be traced back to certain doctrine or elements of the Yugoslav People's Army, but it would take some time to explain this in detail. Well, in short, this principle applies that one person at the top or, rather, one body at the top would combine both political and military functions, thus defining political objectives and military objectives in support of political objectives.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And in a military sense, why -- why is the existence of this unity, why is that important?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because this is an efficient way of attaining the political and military goals on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you. If you could turn, please, to what is at tab 27 of your binder, please. And this is Exhibit P321. And if we could turn, please, to what is ERN R037-6682 at the top. It's the page entitled: "NLA Command and Control." It's page 42 in the Macedonian version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, simply for the assistance of the Registry, I think it's 6862, rather than 6682.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm grateful. If I misspoke, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes, it's 6862.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you see this on the screen, Mr. Bezruchenko?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And this is a page entitled "NLA Command and Control," and we see Ali Ahmeti at the top, and then below him Gzim Ostreni, and then two other gentlemen lower down. But then at the bottom, we see another line with a series of numbers preceded by the letter "G." Can you tell us what this bottom line means and why this is significant for you?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: These bottom lines indicate the structure and organisation of the General Staff. "G" essentially means a certain service within the General Staff. And this is the way any general staff in any army in the world is organised, or at least this is the fact in many cases. "G" normally would stand for personnel -- G1 would generally stand for personnel matters; G2 for intelligence; G3 for operations; G4 for logistics; G5 for civil military matters; G6 for communications; and then come the resources management, and this is the way this General Staff apparently was organised.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Just so that the record is complete, what would G7 refer to?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Management of -- resources management.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And G8?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: This would be, well, essentially the same thing as resources management, I guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. If we can now turn to what is tab 28 in your binder, and in e-court this should be 778 -- 65 ter 778.11. It says "National Liberation Army" at the top, "General Staff," and then in large bold letters -- careful. In large bold letters, it says: "Development of mobilisation," and it should be "personnel," not "personal, "and materiel formation of the General Staff." Do you see that, Mr. Bezruchenko?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we turn to what is page 1 of this document. It's page 2 in the Macedonian version.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And we see a table here. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And there's a title above the table "Basic Mobilisation Plan"?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: M'mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, what is this table and what does it depict?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in any army of the world, any basic organisational unit is structured according to a certain plan, which is sometimes called -- or at least in the West, it is called "The Table of Organisation and Equipment." In some armies of the world, and I think in the former JNA as well, it was "Formation," "Formacija." Well, a basic organisation plan is normally a plan which calls for filling in such formation or tables of organisation and equipment. Just to make it a little bit simple, this is the kind of a plan which determines the number of personnel, equipment and any other resources which would be required for a military unit to function efficiently. This particular document explains how many personnel this unit, in this particular case, the General Staff would have and how it would be organised into departments. As you can see, the departments which are mentioned in this document from G1 to G8 are exactly the same as those mentioned in the previous document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And can you recall who produced this document?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the NLA document, and apparently it was produced by Gzim Ostreni.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I would seek to tender this document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, we'll object at this stage. First, we would wish to know who provided the document in question to the Prosecution or, rather, its origin or chain of custody, as it's called. The second question which we have is also when this document was prepared and whether the Prosecution has any indication at this stage. We believe that if, indeed, this document was or at least is said to have been prepared by Mr. Ostreni, perhaps the best time to seek to tender that document would be when Mr. Ostreni appears as a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, this document was provided to the Office of the Prosecutor on the 29th of July, 2005, and without reviewing Gzim Ostreni's witness statement right now, to the best of my recollection this document was prepared by Mr. Ostreni during 2001.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P486, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bezruchenko, I'd like to ask you, please, to turn to tab 29 in your binder, and this document is Exhibit P00459, Your Honours. If we can just take a look at the first page for a moment, Mr. Bezruchenko. At the top, there's a title "National Liberation Army, General Staff," approved by NLA Commander Ali Ahmeti. And then it says: "Personnel and materiel formation of the brigade." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And if we turn to the next page, please, again I believe we see what you referred to as a table of --

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Organisation and equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Table of organisation and equipment. Thank you. But if I understand correctly, this would be relating to at the level of a brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we could turn, Mr. Bezruchenko, to what is page 7 in the English version and page 5 in the Macedonian version, please.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: We see here, in the middle of this table, we see a reference. It's in bold. It says: "S-1 Personnel Sector," and on the following pages we see: "S-2 Intelligence and Counter-Intelligence Sector," and later on we see, on page 9 of the English version: "S-3 Operations and Training Sector." What does this -- what is the meaning of this letter "S" and the numbers?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again "S" is the letter which stands for various sections at brigade headquarters level, and this indicates the sections which are in charge of certain basic functions of the brigade staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And if I'm understanding you, would the letter "S" in this context have the same function as the letter "G" in the table that we saw for the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's absolutely right. The only difference is the scope of the actual activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we could turn now, please, to --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Before we turn away from this: Again, have you seen such tables at the brigade level before in your career?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Why do you say, "Of course"?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have seen those.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Well, would such tables be common or not amongst armies of the world?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are absolutely common. This is, in fact, one of the most fundamental documents to build up an efficient fighting force.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. If we could turn, please, to what is tab 30 in your binder, Mr. Bezruchenko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, before we move on, if we could ask for assistance from Mr. Saxon and perhaps the witness, whether the Prosecution has any idea of the date at which this document was prepared. The front page suggests the year of 2001, but if Mr. Saxon has any further information about this matter, perhaps through the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I can ask the witness, if you'd like. I don't have any additional information beyond what I gave upon my colleague's previous request.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bezruchenko, do you have any idea when, specifically, in 2001 this document was produced?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not have this idea, but I would imagine that the document was probably produced early in 2001, perhaps January 2001, maybe before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we can go to tab 30, please -- but you're not sure about that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Tab 30 is Exhibit P00460. This is a document, again, it says "National Liberation Army, General Staff" at the top, approved by NLA commander Ali Ahmeti. Here we do see a date, 20 April 2001, and it's entitled -- it should be: "Personnel," not "personal," "and Materiel Formation of the Infantry Battalion." And we see a series of tables in this document, Mr. Bezruchenko. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: This time dealing with battalion command and apparently organisational issues on the battalion level. From a military perspective, why, if at all, is this document significant for you?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is a very significant document, because this is, in fact, the basis and the backbone of the organisation of a basic tactical unit in the field, an infantry battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. And what, if anything, does this document tell you about the structure of the NLA, the overall structure?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it tells me that the NLA apparently had professional military planning documents for building an efficient combat force at its disposal, and apparently the NLA was striving to build such a force on the basis of professional military documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And these documents, what do they tell us, if anything, about the hierarchy of the NLA?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these documents suggest that the NLA had a military hierarchy, well, from the highest level, which was the political and military leadership, to the lowest level, which was apparently an infantry squad. Again, if I could draw a little bit longer on this specific document. This document describes the organisation of an infantry battalion as made up of three infantry companies, a fire support company, and certain support elements. This is a typical structure for an infantry battalion anywhere in the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we can turn, please, to what is tab 31, Mr. Bezruchenko, and this is Exhibit P00461.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Again, this is a document that was provided to the Office of the Prosecutor by Gzim Ostreni. It's entitled "Regulation on the Competencies and Work of the Brigade Command." What is the function and importance of this document, Mr. Bezruchenko?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is, again, an important and one of the fundamentally basic documents in any army in the world which describes the functions, responsibilities and areas of function of activities of brigade officers. As you can see, the document is structured in such a way as to describe the activities, functions and responsibilities of each sector of the brigade staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bezruchenko, can we turn, please, to what is page 3 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is page 4 in the Macedonian version. It would be the next page in the English version, please, and the next page in the Macedonian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bezruchenko, at the top of this page it says "General Provision," but I'd like you, please, to direct your attention to what is the fourth paragraph of this page, which begins with the phrase: "Both written and oral orders ..." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That sentence -- that paragraph says this: "Both written and oral orders are to be carried out without reserve. To carry out the orders they have received, the members of the UCK must contact their direct superiors within a specified period of time." What significance, if any, do you take from this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this paragraph is, in fact, one of the basic requirements of efficient functioning of any army, and this requirement is an agreement of one of the basic principles of the command and control, which is subordination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we turn to the next page, please, in both versions, and we see here, Mr. Bezruchenko, what appears to be a fairly complex organogram. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It's entitled "Structure of the Brigade Command" Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: In your assessment, Mr. Bezruchenko, did the structure of NLA brigades develop to this level of complexity during the crisis time in 2001?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we can turn, please, to the next page, Mr. Bezruchenko, and this is page 6 in the Macedonian version. This page, it says: "3. Commander of the Brigade." And there are a number of provisions here laying out the responsibilities of the brigade commander. We see, in paragraph 3: "With regard to his activities and general state of the brigade, the brigade commander is to be directly responsible to the UCK commander." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Number 6, it says: "He is to organise work throughout the Brigade Command, while carefully respecting rules, regulations and orders from the UCK Command." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And number 7 says: "He is to be ensure and insist that all staff members of the Brigade Command and their direct subordinates carry out their duties and obligations with precision and punctuality and in accordance with periodical, monthly and annual work plans." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Would these responsibilities for a brigade commander, would they be common in armies around the world?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, they would be common.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we can turn, please, Mr. Bezruchenko, to what is paragraph 71 of your amended expert report, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is on the bottom of page 17 of the English version of the amended expert report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Are you at paragraph 71, Mr. Bezruchenko?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And in this section, you had analysed a number of the documents that we've just looked at briefly here, and then you say this in paragraph 71: "Analysis of these documents suggests that NLA leadership was keen to develop NLA brigades as a strong fighting force with emphasis on sabotage and protracted operations." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Help us understand something, please. In a military sense, what does the term "sabotage" mean?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, "sabotage" would essentially be described as a covert operation which would include such things as, for instance, crossing the enemy lines and operating behind the enemy lines, with the goal of blowing up bridges, various vital objectives, capturing prisoners, attacking convoys, attacking headquarters, these kind of things.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And so acts of sabotage, in a military sense, how common are they in modern warfare?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: They're extremely common. If you look back, for instance, to the Second World War, well, each army of the world which was involved in this conflict, specifically say, German forces, British forces, Russian forces, they all used these kind of tactics.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bezruchenko, earlier in your testimony, at page 6067 of the transcript and actually a short time ago today, you used the term -- you refer to something called "asymmetrical warfare," and I should have asked you to define that technical term. Can you explain, please, to the Judges what the term "asymmetrical warfare" means?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, asymmetrical warfare is a recently-developed term or doctrine, if you wish, which describes the type of warfare which would be regarded as opposed to a conventional warfare. Asymmetrical warfare --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can I stop you there?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Maybe this will help us understand. First perhaps if you would -- could you please define what you mean by "conventional warfare"?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are various definitions of "conventional warfare." Some scholars believe conventional warfare is something opposed to nuclear warfare, for instance, but a more common understanding of this term is that conventional warfare is the type of warfare which is common for two opposed armies clashed in the field. The classical example of such warfare would be the First World War or Second World War. Asymmetrical warfare is the term which is ascribed mostly to various partisan, guerrilla or rebel forces which are disadvantaged in terms of weapons and equipment as compared to more better-equipped and better-armed forces and therefore would have to resort to special tactics to relegate these advantages of an adversary force to a level that would actually make it possible for them to carry on fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bezruchenko, why, in 2001, did the NLA need to use tactics of asymmetrical warfare?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because they were not so well equipped. They had weapons which were probably sufficient, but they were not as good as the weapons at the disposal of the government forces. For example, they didn't have combat aircraft. They had no jets, they had no helicopters, and they didn't have enough artillery, long-range artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If you can, please, help us, can you give us a few examples of the asymmetrical tactics that the NLA used during 2001?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: A classical example of asymmetrical tactics in this kind of warfare would be a raid or an ambush. Infiltration is also one of the examples of asymmetrical tactics, in a way. And, in fact, if you are talking specifically about the conflict in Macedonia in 2001, there were at least several examples where the NLA was successful in carrying out ambushes with sufficiently-heavy losses for the Macedonian security forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you to turn your mind, Mr. Bezruchenko, to what is part 3 of your amended expert report. This part is entitled "Government Security Forces." And perhaps if we could start at what is paragraph 218. Your Honours, this is at page 58 of the English version. And I'd like you just to give us -- well, perhaps I can speed this up. Is it correct, Mr. Bezruchenko, in paragraph 218 you explain that section 1 of part 3 describes the structure, organisation, chain of command, strength and weaponry of the Macedonian Army; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And then paragraph 219, you explain that section 2 of part 3 addresses the forces of the Ministry of the Interior. It's the Law on Internal Affairs, Internal Regulations, the structure of the Ministry, the Ministry's chain of command, the powers and authority of the Minister of the Interior, as well as special police units. Is that how you organised your work?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we please turn to paragraph 266, please. This is at the bottom of page 74 in the English version. And before paragraph 266, we see a subtitle, "3.2.4.1". It's titled "Army of the Republic of Macedonia, Command and Control Concept." Can you just tell us, please, briefly, Mr. Bezruchenko, what is the purpose of this section of your report?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the purpose of this section of the report was to describe the command-and-control concept. Well, this section outlines the military hierarchy, the chain of command, and the principles of command and control.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Of the Macedonian Army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Can we please turn to what is paragraph -- it's the next page in the English version. At the bottom, we see paragraph 271. It's a very short paragraph -- actually, it's not, but there's just a sentence -- the first sentence is on page 75 of the English version. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And you refer to seven principles which were listed in a 1983 publication of the Army of the former Republic of Yugoslavia, called "Command and Control." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Starting on the next page, you describe seven principles of command and control, and can you briefly describe these principles to us, please?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these are the principles as they were outlined in the document which you have mentioned, and I believe the same principles were adopted as the basic command-and-control principles in the Army of the Republic of Macedonia. Well, at the top is the principle of single authority. In Macedonian, it is "jednostar jasenstvo", and this is the same word almost in B/C/S as well. And this principle means that there is only one officer who is supposed to give orders to the personnel and units below him and to whom these personnel and units report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: How about the principle of subordination?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is another important principle of the command and control, which in fact was expressed in Macedonian law on defence, and this principle implies an obligation for all military personnel to carry out the orders issued by their superiors.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. You described what is principle number 3, "Unity," previously, so we don't need to review that, but we see principle 4 is "Perpetuity." What does that mean in the military sense?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this means that the principles of command and control, and in fact the actual control of units, well, must be exercised at all times in an absolutely cohesive and an uninterrupted manner, because any disruptions can lead to grave consequences in combat situation, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Principle number 5, "Flexibility," what is that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: This also means that the command and control should be flexible enough to ensure that it functions without interruptions in any situations. Well, perhaps I'm going to explain it a little bit simplistically, but this means that if a commander is to exercise control of his units at all times in combat situation, he should really have various scenarios which might envisage, well, interruption of control, difficult situations, people killed, wounded, and these kind of things, but in spite of that, he must make sure that this happens at all times.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And principle number 6, it's called "Operativeness." What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That means that the commander, when exercising these functions, must in fact be -- I would put it as having a front edge on the adversary. He should plan and exercise his action in such a manner as to respond quickly and adequately to any challenges which may be presented on the battleground by the adversary forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Bezruchenko, the seventh and last principle, "Confidentiality," can you help us with that, please?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is another important principle, which means that the matters of significance in any army of the world must be treated with confidentiality; that is, the documents which are important, well, for various reasons, and there are various rules and regulations which apply to confidentiality and secrecy, must be made inaccessible for anyone besides those personnel which should have the authorised access to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bezruchenko. Paragraphs 272 through 274, you talk a little bit more about these principles, and can you just help us, please. In your assessment, did the officers of the Army of Macedonia -- were they aware of these principles and did they try to implement them?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, they certainly must have been aware of these principles, and they definitely, well, had an obligation to apply these principles.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The next section, which I'm not going to go over with you, section 3.2.4.2, there you describe the role, tasks and structure of the Army of Macedonia, but I'd like to ask you some questions, please, about the second part of part 3, where you talk about the Ministry of the Interior. And if we turn to what is paragraph 369, this is on page 106 in the English version, Your Honours. And before that paragraph, we see -- this is a subsection, 3.3.3, "The Ministry of Interior Command and Control System." Are you with me, Mr. Bezruchenko?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And in paragraph 369, you refer to Article 6 of the Law on Internal Affairs and its relationship to command and control between the Minister of the Interior and the employees of the Ministry. Help us again, please. Why is Article 6 important?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Article 6 reflects the principle of subordination and the system of command and control.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And in 2001, who was the person or position at the top of the Ministry of the Interior, at the top of the chain of command and control?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If you can turn, please, to page 118 of your amended expert report in the English version. It's paragraph 424. There is a subsection here, 3.3.3.7, titled "Disciplinary Powers," and in paragraph 424 you refer to Article 65 of the Law on Internal Affairs. It's a description of types of violations of labour discipline, and the minister's responsibility regarding the dismissal of employees." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we turn to the next page, paragraph 425, and this is at page 106 in the Macedonian version, and paragraph 425 you quote from Article 65 of the Law on Internal Affairs: "More severe cases of violation of labour discipline, for which a worker may be relieved from the work, the length of the dismissal deadline, as well as cases which do not grant the right to such deadline shall be formulated with a legal act issued by the minister." What, if anything, do you find significant in that article, please?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: My reading of this article would be as follows: It is the minister who would have the rights to decide to relieve an employee of the Ministry of his duties, as well as to decide when such action would need to be taken. I would also say that this action would need to be reflected in a legal act issued by the minister, most probably an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm about to go on to another topic. Would this be an appropriate time to take the first break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will. Very well, Mr. Saxon, we will have the break and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bezruchenko, could you please turn to page 122 of the English version of the amended expert report. We're going to be looking at paragraph 441. It's the first paragraph beneath a subtitle -- subsection 3.3.4.2 called "Special Police Unit 'Lions '." Are you there, please?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Just very briefly, according to your review and your research. What events led to the formation of the unit that became known as the Lions?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: At some point of the conflict, it has become abundantly clear that there was something wrong with the strategy used by the Macedonian security forces. The conflict began sometime in January 2001, and all the time until August there was no decisive defeat inflicted on the NLA. I think the Macedonian public became especially frustrated after the battle of Aracinovo which was the indication that the NLA was capable of establishing its base in the immediate vicinity of the capital, which was a pretty dangerous development, so apparently at the very top of the Macedonian political establishment it was decided that additional forces were required which would be specifically trained and equipped for asymmetrical warfare and counter-insurgency operations. This consideration probably led to the decision to establish a special police unit which later received the name Lions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The battle at Aracinovo that you mentioned, that took place in the last part of June 2001; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: In fact, the NLA entered Aracinovo on or about 9 June 2001, and the battle took place in the next two weeks to follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If you can turn, please, Mr. Bezruchenko, to the start of part 4 of your report, and it's on page 129 of the English version -- excuse me, 128 of the English version. Part 4 is entitled "The attack on Ljuboten," 10 to 12 August 2001. And is it right, Mr. Bezruchenko, in this section, this part of the report, you summarise the information available related to the events in Ljuboten on that weekend from the documents that you had available to you?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If you could turn, please, to paragraph 484. It's page 129 of the English version. In that paragraph, you discuss the degree of active resistance from the village of Ljuboten on the 12th of August, and you say in the very first sent sentence, that the degree of resistance is hard to measure. But then you say this in the last sentence: "Assuming that combat casualties normally serve as the main indicator of the degree of an adversary's level of armed resistance, the level of resistance from Ljuboten to Tarculovski's group on 12th August was probably light to nonexistent." Can you explain to the Judges how you came to this opinion?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many Macedonian military documents suggest that there was fire coming out of Ljuboten levelled at the Macedonian security forces. However, it is difficult to measure what kind of volume of the fire was. Macedonian military documents suggest that there was at least a number of military targets in Ljuboten, among them a machine-gun, but given the fact that there were no casualties among the Macedonian military forces, well, it would be difficult to measure what kind of exact degree of resistance was offered from the village. So my conclusion was that it was probably light.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Let me ask the question perhaps in a slightly different way. If the members of the security forces of Macedonia had received heavy casualties in Ljuboten on that weekend, what would your conclusion have been? Would it have been different?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it would have been different. My conclusion in this case would be that the village was heavily protected and whatever group -- the NLA group could have been there would have been well armed and organised.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Bezruchenko, can you briefly describe to the Judges what is part 5 of your report, please?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Part 5 of my report represents the chronology of the conflict, and this chronology was drawn on the basis of various documents which, among others, included media reports, Macedonian military documents, Macedonian police documents and some NLA documents as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And this chronology relates to -- includes events from January to October 2001?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. Well, more precise, the bulk of this chronology relates to January and September 2001, and as we know, September 26 was the date when the NLA officially announced that it was disbanded.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And what was your purpose in creating this chronology?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in military analysis chronology is an important instrument which suggests the concept of the operations, how the operations were evolving on the ground, and what were the political or military objectives behind these operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Would a chronology also relate to the intensity of a conflict?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course it would.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Now, it's my turn. Mr. Bezruchenko, if you can go back to the binder with exhibits, please, and if you could turn to what is tab 32 in the binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is 65 ter number 159. It was received from Gzim Ostreni in 2005. And, Your Honour, this exhibit, for lack of a better word, actually has two parts, and the first part I'd like to show to the witness is a map, and I believe that you should have a colour copy of this map in your binder. And this is the map that I hope that you have. At least that was the plan, anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And perhaps if you could pull out the map, Mr. Bezruchenko. And we see the word "Direktive" in big, bold letters on the upper left-hand side. We see a date on the upper right-hand corner, "13 June 2001". And then towards the bottom of the page, we see a blue stamp and the words above that "Komandant," and then we see the signature of Ali Ahmeti there. And, Mr. Bezruchenko, if you could describe to the Judges -- if you could describe what this map shows, perhaps starting with the yellow colour that we see on the upper left-hand portion.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an operational planning document, and it represents essentially the concept of NLA operations as devised, as we can see from the date, 13th June 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: At about that time, what was going on sort of globally with respect to the conflict? Where was the NLA?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The NLA was advancing and regrouping itself, and the fighting was continuing despite the attempts to arrange cease-fire. The yellow colour would indicate the areas which were easily under NLA control or at least to where the NLA could move without significant hindrance. The green colour would indicate the axis of advance that were planned for the NLA to move along.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you indicate what this map seems to indicate in terms of the intended axis of advance, following this green colour?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally speaking, this means that the NLA was planning to advance further deep into the country from north and from west. As we can see, the main axis of advance were planned to be from Tetovo to the east towards the capital of Skopje, in the area of Kumanovo. You can see two prongs from the north and from the south, which were apparently aimed to encircle Kumanovo. In the west, you can see several prongs from the area adjacent to the border with Albania to the east in the direction of Gostivar and further Kicevo, and in the south we again see a number of prongs aimed for Ohrid.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And by looking at this plan from a military perspective, what objective or objectives can you assess from this plan? What was the NLA trying to do?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The NLA was trying to grab as much territory as possible and put it under its control.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. If we can turn to the document that accompanies this map, and it's also in your binders, Your Honours. It has a heading at the top "Ideas for Conducting the Operation."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bezruchenko, the first paragraph under this heading says that: "While continuing to increase the number of units in the brigades in line with the establishment, active combat operations will be undertaken with a view to breaking up and eliminating the enemy's troops, so as to block and take over the towns and main roads of Western Macedonia as rapidly as possible." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It says that: "The Skopje-Debar, Skopje-Kicevo-Struga roads will be blocked, making enemy communications impossible, and it says then, in phase 1, the blockades would be erected in the area of the village of Grupcin, Mavrova, Gryka e Derventes/Derventska Klisura, et cetera. So what does this paragraph of the plan indicate?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is the fundamental idea of the concept of the operation which was based apparently on three major objectives: To break up the Macedonian security forces; to occupy main towns in Western Macedonia; and to deny the capabilities of moving and manoeuvring of the Macedonian security forces along the main roads in the country, at least in its western part.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: We see down below it says: "The operation will be conducted in two stages." You see stage 1 by 10 July, stage 2 by the end of July. To your knowledge, was the NLA successful in completing these stages by the given dates?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we can turn, please, to the next page in the English version, which will be page 2 in the Macedonian version. And at the top of the next page, we see a section four with the subtitle "Deployment and Tasks of UCK Forces." Do you see that, Mr. Bezruchenko?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And it begins: "The 113th Brigade will, by 10 July 2001, make preparations to capture or cut off the town of Kumanova and block the Kumanova-Kriva Palanka and Kumanova-Sveti Nikole roads." Below that -- I won't go on yet. Did the NLA succeed in capturing Kumanovo at that time?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: But what did it succeed in doing with respect to Kumanovo?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The situation in the area of Kumanovo was pretty serious. The NLA managed to establish control over a number of villages in the area and was gradually expanding its control. I believe that with time passing by, they probably could indeed reach the objective of cutting the road between Kumanovo and Kriva Palanka.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The next paragraph says: "At the same time, the 113th Brigade troops holding the village of Aracinovo will form the 1st Battalion of the 114th Brigade, and gradually continue recruiting to full strength at brigade level with personnel and fighters from Skopje and villages in the northern part of Skopje, as well as the villages south of Kumanova." From a military perspective, what do you take from this? What is happening here?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: This indicates a pretty serious development. This indicates that the NLA, (a), was building up another brigade and, (b), and this brigade was supposed to operate in the area of the capital.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. The next paragraph talks about the 115th Brigade's battalion in the Derventa area, saying: " ... will continue efforts to expand at brigade level, also forming a 2nd Battalion in the Karsijak area and beyond ..." And then it talks about preparations to take over additional areas. What, if anything, do you see significant about these instructions?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the significance of this particular paragraph is that it provides instruction for the 115th Brigade to expand and form another battalion in the area of Zadem [phoen] which is another mountain feature between Tetovo and Skopje. And as we know from the chronology, there was a very successful ambush carried out by NLA in this very area on the 8th of August. So the significance of this paragraph, to briefly emphasise it again, is that this 115th Brigade was actually being raised to cut the communication between Tetovo and Skopje, which is again classical military tactics and operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Just so that the record is clear, did you mean the 115th Brigade or this battalion of the 115th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is apparent from this paragraph that the 115th Brigade was in the process of building up its forces, so I'm talking about 115th Brigade here as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. The next paragraph, we see that: "The 112th Brigade in the area to the west of Tetova will send a company to close the Skopje-Tetova road in the area of Grupcin village." To your knowledge, did that occur at some point?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not certain if this particular event did occur, but I know that the NLA forces were indeed operating in the area of Mountain Zadem as I mentioned previously. Whether it was the 112th Brigade or the 115th is difficult to establish, but I would be inclined to believe it was the 115th.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Indeed, this paragraph mentions both the 112th and 115th Brigades.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, which may suggest that these two brigades were cooperating in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If you could turn to the next page, please, Mr. Bezruchenko. There's a subtitle here called "Balance of Forces." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And it says: "The balance of forces on the Western Macedonia front is currently a 1:5 ratio in favour of the government troops, and they are greatly superior in terms of equipment, but by towards the end of July, it will still be 1:2 in favour of the government forces, and in the field of equipment, tank, aircraft units, et cetera, it will remain the same." And then it says: "The morale of the UCK forces plays a significant role in ameliorating the balance of forces between the government forces and the UCK and will alter the ratio to a proportion of 1:10 in favour of the UCK infantry." What is your assessment of what is being said here?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: My reading of this paragraph would be to suggest that apparently the government's security forces indeed had the numeric preponderance of the NLA in the Western Macedonia, but due to the process of reinforcement being brought in, as well as building up of the NLA units, the ratio of forces was rapidly changing and declining in favour of the NLA. This paragraph also speaks about high morale of the NLA forces, which allegedly ensures superiority over the NLA -- I mean, over the security forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And in your research to write your report, what did you learn about the level of morale of the NLA forces as opposed to the level of moral of the Macedonian security forces?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have come across a number of military documents in the process of writing my reports which suggest that the level of morale of the NLA was indeed quite high and at times was superior to that of the Macedonian military forces. I have also read some Macedonian military documents which tend to suggest that the mobilisation effort generally was considered as unsuccessful, meaning that the morale of the troops which were supposed to be mobilised and dispatched to the front was not really at the appropriate level.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bezruchenko, just so that the record is clear, when you referred to the mobilisation effort just now, were you referring to the efforts by the Macedonian government to mobilise more men or by the NLA?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm referring to the efforts of the Macedonian government.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Down below we see a paragraph related to anti-aircraft defence potential. If you could turn to the next page, Mr. Bezruchenko, or last page, there is a sentence. It's the last sentence. It's page 4 in the Macedonian version. It says: "International Conventions must be strictly respected during all operations by UCK troops, and the treatment of civilians and facilities must be at the required level." Why is this important for an army?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The respect for international conventions in times of war is an important factor which contributes, (a), to the morale of fighting forces and, (b), makes it a legitimate force. Therefore, in brief, I would say that it was very important for the NLA to maintain the level of discipline and to ensure that the respect for the Geneva Conventions would be at the appropriate level.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would seek to tender this map and the written texts that accompany it, please, into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P487, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
