utterances.text: If you could turn, Mr. Bezruchenko, to what is tab 33 in your binder, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is 65 ter number 611.1. Before I go on, that last exhibit is referred to in Mr. Bezruchenko's report at footnotes 34, 143, 236, 237, that's the map, and the ideas for conducting the operation in footnotes 79, 130, 131, 136 and 143. Mr. Bezruchenko, 65 ter number 611.1 is another map. It was obtained from the archives of the Ministry of Defence of Macedonia, February of 2006. Your Honours, it is referred to at pages 400 -- excuse me, footnote 434 of Mr. Bezruchenko's amended expert report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Briefly, Mr. Bezruchenko, what do we see on this map in front of us? What does it say at the top?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the top, it says "The decision of the Commander of the 1st Guards Brigade for Defence."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And what do these markings on the map indicate? We see markings in red, with bits of yellow, and then we see markings in blue.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The markings in blue stand for the position -- positions of the Macedonian security forces. In this particular case, this is the 1st Guards Brigade, and on the extreme left of its zone -- sorry, on the extreme right of its zone of responsibility, you see the zone of the 3rd Guards Battalion. The red markings represent the NLA forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: We see some arrows. If we can perhaps focus on the red markings on the upper right-hand side of the document. We see some red arrows going from top towards the bottom. What do these red arrows indicate?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: These arrows indicate the axis of advance of the NLA forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: From what area towards what area?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: From north, in this particular case obviously from the area of Kumanovo, towards southwest, towards the capital, and again from west in the direction of east again towards the capital.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And based on your knowledge and the other documents that you have seen, can you give an estimate of when this map would have been created or the time period that it reflects?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Early June 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And we see on the bottom right-hand side that it is stamped with the signature of the commander who apparently produced this map. Your Honours, I would seek to tender this map, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, we will not object to the tendering of that document at this stage, but we would like to place it on the record that three different witnesses were members of this particular organisation, were called by the Prosecution at the time, and were not put the document or asked to provide any information in particular as regard the time or as regard the other matters that have been commented upon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P488, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Finally, Mr. Bezruchenko, could you please turn to what is tab 36 in your binder, and this is marked for identification Exhibit P00464, Your Honours. It is referred to in footnotes 4, 27 and 28, 41, 137, 315, 327, 463 and 465 of the amended expert report, and at footnotes 1, 4, 5 and 8 of the amended addendum to the expert report. And you saw this, part of this exhibit briefly, Your Honours, with witness Nazim Bushi. This is a book entitled "The War in Macedonia in 2001". I take it you're familiar with this book, Mr. Bezruchenko?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And who are the authors of this book?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The authors of this book are recognised Macedonian military experts, former Chief of General Staff and doctor, Mitre Arsovski, and his colleagues, Kuzev and Damjanovski and I believe Mr. Kuzev is a colonel and Mr. Damjanovski is a general.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'd like to discuss with you briefly several portions of this book which have been translated into English, and perhaps if I can ask the assistance of the Court Officer. If we can call up the portion that has the ERN range N006-3017 to N006-3033. And this page here is actually page 96, for those who are following along in the Macedonian version, and this part of the book, this chapter, is entitled "Measures of the Competent Organs of the Government in the Field of Defence." Are you with me, Mr. Bezruchenko?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Could we turn, please, to what is page 7 in the English version. It is the bottom of page 105 in the Macedonian version. That's it. And if we could focus on the bottom of the page, please, for now. This is a subsection entitled: "The government of the Republic of Macedonia," and it says that: "The government of the Republic of Macedonia, as bearer of the executive government of the Republic, has a very prominent role in the field of defence."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: "In addition to proposing the most significant documents in this field, it is also responsible for submitting numerous regulations and decisions that regulate specific segments of the defence system and the armed forces." And then there's a reference, we see, to the Law on Defence, and -- we see at the beginning here a list at the bottom of page 7 of the responsibilities of the Government of Macedonia in this regard. If we could turn to the next page in the English version and to the bottom of page 106 in the Macedonian version, and this portion of the book is referred to at paragraph 402(a) in the amended addendum to the amended expert report. Do you see, Mr. Bezruchenko, we see in the middle of the page, above the bold line, it says: "Not all of the government's responsibilities enacted in the Law are listed below, since some of them were explained in other sections. As a result, only part of them are listed here." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And it says in bold: "Orders the use of the police during martial law to support the army." And it says: "It is immediately noticeable that the police is used to support the army during martial law." But then it tells us: "In 2001, the government fully adhered to this regulation in the Law on Defence and ordered the police to be used in a time of war, though without declaring martial law." And then it says: "All of the misunderstandings between the police and army originated precisely from this." The next paragraph tells us this: "Since martial law was not declared, the police was not under joint command and acted independently. One can only imagine what the situation is like when two ministers from the same government, Ministry of the Interior and Ministry of Defence, have two armed components at their disposal, one of which is 'commanded'," in quotes, "by the Prime Minister through the Ministry of the Interior, while the other is under the command of the President of the Republic through the Defence Minister." You told us a bit before about the importance of unity of command. What does this paragraph suggest to you in terms of how well the security forces were functioning at that time?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Apparently there were certain discrepancies in the functioning of the chain of command of the Macedonian security forces. Apparently the Macedonian authorities failed to establish a single centre of command which would be in charge of operations of both the army and the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The next paragraph, it says: "The two ministers, from differing political provenances, rather than enduring on the course of joint defence of national and state interests in such a complicated and dangerous security situation, seemed to be 'fighting' for elevated positions in their parties, the government and the defence." And then it says: "As a result, it could be said that the two armed structures - the police and the army - were each fighting on their own front. This type of deployment of the police, as the Prime Minister's armed force, caused a rift in the management and command of the joint security forces of the Republic of Macedonia." Would it appear, Mr. Bezruchenko, that the authors of this book and you would agree as to the results of these kinds of conflicts?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I fully concur with the conclusions of the authors of this book.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we can turn now, please, to another portion of this book which has the ERN range N006-3064 to N006-3067. And it begins at page 143 in the Macedonian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Are you with me, Mr. Bezruchenko?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The top paragraph says this: "Apart from the fact that the then-valid Law on Defence clearly regulated the use of the police in wartime conditions, during our war, there were different and opposing views on who controls and commands the police." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It's the top of that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not entirely certain if we are on the same page here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you read it on the screen?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the middle of the page, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bezruchenko, can you look at me, please?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: This is what the page looks like. It says: "Deployment of the armed forces on the front."

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you look at the paragraph above that, please?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And it says that there were -- it says: " ... During our war," at the top, "there were different and opposing views on who controls and commands the police." Do you see that sentence, the third and fourth line down from the top. Mr. Bezruchenko, if you look at the third line from the top, you'll see a phrase that says "during our war."

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see it, sir. It's probably the right -- the wrong page.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Well, your page should have at the top of it an ERN number N006-3064. Can you go to the next portion of the report, please,?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Or if the usher could assist me. If the usher could provide me with Mr. Bezruchenko's binder, I will turn to the page. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If you look -- if you could look at what I've just highlighted, Mr. Bezruchenko.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You see it says: " ... During our war, there were different and opposing views on who controls and commands the police."

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And then a little bit later, it says this: "In a state of war, the police shall be used to carry out combat tasks as an integral part of the army."

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: "This article of the Law on Defence was clear to everyone except the politicians of 'relevant' parties in power."

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: "However, the fact remained that there was duality in command and control, because the Prime Minister commanded the police through the Minister of the Interior, while the Supreme Commander commanded the Army. This is why there were many uncoordinated combat operations in the war, which contributed to greater casualties, the loss of whole battles and struggles, and even the war as a whole." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, I see that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Help us understand something, please. This phrase "duality in command and control," what does that mean? What does it usually mean?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: This would describe two or more chains of command in cases where the command-and-control system would be disrupted, and resulting in multiple chains of command, whereas in fact only one should exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. If we can turn to the next page, please, in the English version. This is page 145 in the Macedonian version. There is a paragraph in the middle of the page, Mr. Bezruchenko. It begins with the phrase: "We have to point out ..." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It says: "We have to point out that during the war there was a wise reticence of the President of Parliament, and Parliament did not declare whether Macedonia was in a state of war or not. Only then does it become perfectly clear why there were such a difference of views in the sphere of command and control of the army and the police." And in the next paragraph, we're told: "In the broad coalition government, the Defence Minister was from the SDSM Party, the Minister of the Interior from the VMRO-DPMNE Party, and the Minister of Justice from the DPA." And later on: "The Minister of Defence had carte blanche for command and control of the army, stipulated by law." And then we're told: "On the other hand, the Minister of the Interior did not wish to remain without an 'army', so besides having the legal part of the police, following a government decision, he established an illegal unit called the Lions, promoting the president into its unlawful supreme commander. As such, he did not want to subordinate to the lawful Supreme Commander by fighting with his own army (the police), making his own decisions, tactical variants, and fighting in the territory of his choice and with his own opponent." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Would this be another or a particular example of so-called duality of command?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a typical one, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, there was one portion of this book that was shown to you during the testimony -- redirect examination of witness Nazim Bushi, and those are the conclusions. And I'd just like to briefly look at one page of that. This portion of the book has ERN version -- ERN range N006-3325 to N006-3334. If we can turn to what is the third page in the English version, and it's page 407 in the Macedonian version, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you see paragraph 7 there? This should be the last portion of this book that you have in your binder.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: M'mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And it says "Conclusions" at the top.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If you turn to the third page, please, paragraph 7 at the top, and it says this -- do you see paragraph 7?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: "The belligerent forces which the Republic of Macedonia set its security forces against were varied, but they were united in terms of their ultimate goal." And then later on it says: "Together they represented a joint armed force of an imaginary Greater Albania. Therefore we can conclude that Macedonia was essentially in an informal war with Albania and its fundamental goal of uniting all Albanians in the Balkans in one state." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: My question for you is simply this: In your assessment, was the principle of unity of command in effect with the NLA forces?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would seek to tender now what has been marked for identification as P464.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Under the same number, Exhibit P464, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bezruchenko, I have no further questions for you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Bezruchenko. My name is Guenael Mettraux, and I'm appearing on behalf of Mr. Boskoski.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Mr. Bezruchenko, you will recall that on the first day of your examination-in-chief, you were asked a number of questions from Mr. Saxon about a concept known as "operational control." Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And in your evidence-in-chief, you indicated that in your view, the concept or doctrine of operational control, according to that doctrine, "the minister is", and I quote, "The one who is ultimately responsible for all operations, actions of the Ministry, as well as his subordinate personnel." Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And you recall that upon an objection by the Defence, Mr. Saxon indicated that your discussion of this concept, the doctrine of operational control, was discussed in, I believe, paragraph 3.3.3.1 of your report; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And I would simply like to draw your attention to a particular paragraph of that report which is contained in that section. That is paragraph 371 of the report, at which you say the following: "Several Macedonian Ministry of Interior documents suggest that Minister of Interior Boskoski exercised operational control of police forces, which was manifested in orders to deploy police at crisis areas." Mr. Bezruchenko, do you recall making that statement or would you wish to see the report?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would be grateful to Your Honour if you could give me a chance to find this particular section of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Mr. Bezruchenko, that will be page 107 of your report, and that's paragraph 371.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is Exhibit P466 perhaps for your assistance.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm at page 107 now, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bezruchenko. And if I could ask you to look at what is paragraph 371, please.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And simply to refresh your memory about a statement you make in this report, you said the following: "Several Macedonian Ministry of Interior documents suggest that Minister of Interior Boskoski exercised operational control of police forces, which was manifested in orders to deploy police at various crisis areas." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And do you recall making that statement --

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: -- in your report? Is it correct, Mr. Bezruchenko, and please correct me if I'm wrong, that the supposed relevance of your evidence on that particular issue or the issue of so-called operational control, is to suggest that at the relevant time Minister of Interior Boskoski was somehow able to exercise control of police forces during police operations; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you believe a certain -- I mean, if you assume that a certain function of operational control is deployment of forces on the ground, that is exactly the case, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And as you just indicated, this doctrine or theory would, as one of its elements, require that the transfer of people or members of a particular entity to another location be part of the -- or be evidence, if you wish, of operational control; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And your evidence on that point, Mr. Bezruchenko, is based on your military expertise; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And I think you've indicated, in response to a question of Mr. Saxon, that the definitions which you've used -- or at least I think you made the point in relation to armed conflict, that definitions which you used are military definitions; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And this would apply in particular to the concept of operational control; is it correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And I think you indicated, again I believe it's in response to a question by Mr. Saxon asked during your first day of examination, about ARMED conflict in particular, that you had relied on the military definition of that concept, and for that purpose you had relied upon a particular publication of, I believe, the Department of Defence of the United States. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And that publication would be the Joint Publication 1-02 of the Department of Defence; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And do you agree or are you aware of the fact that this particular document, the so-called Joint Publication, JP1-02, also contains a definition of what constitutes operational control?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And as you did with the definition of "armed conflict," would you regard this definition as generally reliable about what would constitute operational control?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And I would like to ask you or, rather, to show you that definition, Mr. Bezruchenko. You are quite familiar with it, but it may assist others.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And if I can ask the Registry to bring up what is Rule 65 ter 1D928. The ERN range is 1D00-7874, 1D00-7885. Your Honours, simply for the record, the document in its entirety is several hundred pages' long. We have uploaded parts of the document which contain a number of definitions or terms which we may wish to present to ask comments about from Mr. Bezruchenko. I would ask the Registry, please, to turn to page 391 of that document. That would be page 1D00-7885. 883; I apologise. And if the Registry could scroll down a bit on the page. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Mr. Bezruchenko, do you have in front of you the entry, so to say, which defines the concept of operational control?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And I'd like to read it, and if you can follow with me, please, Mr. Bezruchenko, I will ask you a few questions about this. The definition of that concept is as follows: "Operational control. Command authority that may be exercised by commanders at any echelon at or below the level of combatant command." And I will just stop here for a second. Is that correct that in military doctrine, the concept of operational control only applies at a particular level of the military hierarchy; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it really depends on what you mean by "any particular level of military hierarchy."

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, is it correct that at least as far as the US or DOD definition of the concept is concerned, the concept or the doctrine of operational control would apply only at echelons which are at or below the level of combatant command; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, or we can say, in fact, not necessarily combatant command, but any institution involved in the combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, if we stick for a minute with this particular definition, Mr. Bezruchenko, we'll see later about the possibility of applying this to other circumstances. But will you agree that as far as the definition given by the DOD which I understand applies to all branches of the American army, the doctrine of operational control would only apply at or below the level of combat command -- combatant command; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what the document says, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And is that a fact that you felt you should mention in your report, and did you do so?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Then the definition goes on to say this: "Operational control is the authority to perform those functions of command over subordinate forces involving organising and employing command and forces, assigning tasks, designating objectives, and giving authoritative direction necessary to accomplish the mission. Operational control includes authoritative direction over all aspects of military operations and joint training necessary to accomplish missions assigned to the command. "Operational control should be exercised through the commanders of subordinate organisations. Normally this authority is exercised through subordinate joint force commanders and service and/or functional component commanders. Operational control normally provides full authority to organise commands and forces and to employ those forces as the commander in operational control considers necessary to accomplish assigned missions; it does not, in and of itself, include authoritative directions for logistics or matters of administration, discipline, internal organisation, or unit training." Before I ask you a number of questions about this particular definition, Mr. Bezruchenko, you've just indicated your belief that you had made -- or you have given an indication in your report that this doctrine would not apply at or below the level of combatant command, and would you recall in what part of that -- of your report this note would be, if you can recall?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that I made any direct reference, well, to this particular document in my report, but essentially the whole of my report was based on the concept of operational control as stipulated in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: So in answer to the question, you haven't specifically addressed the fact that this doctrine, at least as far as this particular definition is concerned, only applies at a certain level of the hierarchy in the military; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a common knowledge among military experts, I would -- if I may say so, and I don't really think that it really warrants to make any references to this particular document. This is essentially a compilation of military terms which everyone is aware of.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters kindly ask that a pause be maintained between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Mr. Bezruchenko, we've been warned for the first time, about pausing between question and answer, that is.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Is it correct, Mr. Bezruchenko, as you've just indicated, that in fact you do not make any reference to that particular document, and I'm talking about the documents we're looking at right now and which you say you have used, at least as far as the definition of "armed conflict" is concerned, there is no reference to that document in your report; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you specifically mean, sir, whether I quote this particular document in my report and whether it is mentioned in any of the footnotes, the answer, to the best of my knowledge, is "no."

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I'm grateful for that, Mr. Bezruchenko. Is it correct that if one looks at this particular definition of what the concept of operational control is, it refers, in various parts, to, I think, the idea of operation, operational, and also mission. Is that correct, that's what it refers to?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And is that correct also --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Sorry. Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm very sorry to interrupt. To assist the interpreters, I've been signaled that it might be helpful if Mr. Bezruchenko could sit a little bit further away from the microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I'm grateful to Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Mr. Bezruchenko, is that correct that the concept of operation, which you've used in several parts of your report or made reference to, is also a military concept?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is indeed, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And the concept which you've used or the way in which you've utilised this concept is again you've used it in military fashion; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And if the Registry could go to the previous page of the document that is now on the screen. That would be formally page 390 of the entire document, and it's 1D00-7882.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And, Mr. Bezruchenko, if I can ask you to focus on the last entry of that document. There is an entry called "Operation." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And I will read to you the definition which the Department of Defence of the United States gives of that concept in military doctrine. It says this: "1. A military action or the carrying out of a strategic, operational, tactical, service, training, or administrative military mission." Then: "2. The process of carrying on combat, including movement, supply, attack, defence, and manoeuvres needed to gain the objectives of any battle or campaign." And I suppose you will agree that this is again a pretty classical definition of the concept of operation in military doctrine. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And what it refers to in paragraph or number 1 and 2 is "Military mission" in 1, and more specifically the process of carrying out combat in number 2; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And again your conclusions and findings in that regard were military in nature, based on your military expertise; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And can you agree, Mr. Bezruchenko, with the suggestions that orders given, for instance, to provide fire support, in the context of, say, a military mission, or orders to use troops in combat, would be an indication or would be perhaps even evidence of the possibility that operational control is being exercised? Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with that, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters kindly ask the witness to maintain a pause before responding.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, would that be a convenient time or is it 12.30?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We would normally run to 12.30. We --

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: It's my fault, Your Honour. I believed it was 12.15. I will continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We use diminishing periods, because counsel and witnesses increasingly tire during the period, so that the later period is longer than the first.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I think it's a wise course, Your Honour. I'll continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Mr. Bezruchenko, in your report you've applied the concept or the doctrine of operational control to the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Macedonia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, sir. If I may comment on that at this point. The reason for that being the simple fact that the forces of the Ministry of Interior were involved in the war on Macedonia in 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, I'm grateful for that, Mr. Bezruchenko. I will ask you this question, then: Are you aware of a particular law or a particular regulation that is applicable to the Ministry of Interior and which relies upon the concept of operational control?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: My question -- sorry, my answer to this question would be as follows: In fact, the whole concept of functioning and hierarchy, as well as the operational control, of the Ministry of Interior is fundamentally described in the Law on Internal Affairs of the Republic of Macedonia, and in a sense these fundamentals do not necessarily differ from the fundamentals of the command and control as described in the Law on Defence of the Republic of Macedonia. There are the same three basic principles there; the single authority, subordination, and the unity of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, if I can ask you simply to answer the previous question, Mr. Bezruchenko. Are you aware, through your research or the review of the material which you have reviewed or consulted for the purpose of preparing your report or otherwise, come across a reference to the doctrine or the theory of operational control as would be applicable to the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't quite understand what you actually mean, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, my question is this: You have indicated in your report and in evidence that this particular doctrine, which is, as you indicated, a military sort of doctrine called "operational control," would be applicable in your view to the functioning and structure or mechanism of the Ministry of Interior, and my question, it's only a preliminary question, is whether in your review of the material in particular -- I should qualify that. In your review of the laws and regulations that are applicable to the Ministry of Interior, you have come across this particular doctrine or this particular theory in the form of a statement to the effect that it would be applicable to the Ministry of the interior?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The definition of "operational control," as provided by this specific document, is in fact a military definition and is also an academic definition, if you wish. But answering your question more specifically, if I came across any documents related to operational control as applied to the Ministry of Interior, I would say, yes, there is at least one book of rules which describes essentially the operations of the Ministry of Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, I'm grateful for that, and this was the next question I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: The rule of book [sic] is Exhibit P96, and if the witness could be shown that document, please. This would be R042-4624-ET-01 in the English, and the Macedonian would be R042-4623-01, I believe. Mr. Bezruchenko, is it the particular document which you have just referred to?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you kindly go to the next page?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: In the English or the Macedonian?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Could the Registry assist, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, this is this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And if I could ask the Registry to turn to Article 154 of the rule of books. I believe this would be page R042-4643-ET-02 [Realtime transcript read in error "R042-4643-80-02"] in the English. It would be -- I will repeat. It would be R042-4643-ET - England and Tom - -02, and in the Macedonian this would be R042-4623-22. Do you have Article 154 in front of you, Mr. Bezruchenko?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And if I can ask you to direct your attention to the, if you wish, the third indented part of that article, it starts with the words: "Direct preventive engagement by the authorised officials ..." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And if you go further in the text of that provision, you will see a reference in the English version to: "... operational control over dangerous areas ..." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And I will ask your assistance in the Macedonian now, which I believe you have on the other side of the screen, and look at the same article. Can you see that particular passage, the same passage we just looked at, Mr. Bezruchenko?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please read this -- kindly read this passage again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Certainly, at least in the English, Mr. Bezruchenko. This starts with the words: "Direct preventative engagement by the authorised officials by undertaking appropriate measures for physically averting an attack ..." And it goes on, and in approximately the middle of that paragraph, there's a reference to something called "operational control over dangerous areas." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And can I ask you, Mr. Bezruchenko, please, to locate the same passage in the Macedonian version.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you could be a little bit -- I mean if it could be a little bit magnified somehow.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Could the Registry --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters kindly ask the witness to pull up the microphone so we can hear, and kindly maintain a pause before answering.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: You're being asked to do many things at the same time. Perhaps I should give the paper copy to Mr. Bezruchenko.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: If you can look at the -- it's again Article 154. It's the second indented part of that document, and I believe I have highlighted in blue part of that.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Can you see that, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Is it correct that, in fact, the original Macedonian refers not to operational control but to operative control, "operativna kontrol"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It can be translated both ways, but semantically I don't really see any big difference here.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Perhaps I should ask you this, then: Are you aware of any internal regulations or instructions of the Ministry of Interior which contain a definition of the concept of operational -- let me ask you first, of operational control? Are you aware of any documents similar in kind, if you wish, to the one from the DOD which would contain a definition of operational control? Are you aware of any such documents?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you specifically referring to Macedonian Ministry of Interior, sir, or do you mean documents in general?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: No, I apologise. About the Ministry of Interior in particular, Mr. Bezruchenko.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Operational control related to the Ministry of Interior. No, I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Are you aware of any particular internal instructions or regulations applicable to the Ministry of Interior which refer to the concept of operative control?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there is a number of such documents, and in fact one of those which is the one that I'm holding in my hands now.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And you agree that the definitions used by the Ministry of Interior actually all refer to that concept of operative control as I cited from the original, and you will correct me, it's "operativna kontrol"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't really see, again as I mentioned, really any serious difference between "operativna" which is in Macedonian, and "operational" which is in English. In fact, these two notions, expressed in different languages, of course, essentially apply to the same idea, which is control, well, for execution of a certain mission. It's just to put it simply.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please move closer to the microphones, because the interpreters cannot hear him, anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I apologise to the interpreter for cutting off.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Mr. Bezruchenko, the view that you just expressed, is that a personal view of yours or is that something you say, you base on particular material and regulation of the Ministry of Interior of which you are aware of?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And when you gave this definition or made this distinction which in your view applies between the concept of operational and operative, which document in particular would you be referring to?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for instance, the one which I'm holding now.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And you agree that all of those documents refer to "operativni," "operative"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not necessarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Are you aware of a document that would refer to what would be -- I apologise. You will excuse me for the accent -- to something called "operacijonalni kontrol" "operational control." Are you aware of any documents containing those words?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir. This is a purely semantical thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Perhaps I will simply move on and ask you this question for the last -- simply to clear up the matter. Is that your evidence that you are not aware of any regulations or internal instructions applicable to the Ministry of Interior where that particular concept of operational control is defined; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you are specifically referring, sir, to what is termed in Macedonian as "operacijonalni kontrol," no, I didn't see anything like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bezruchenko. Is that correct also that in --

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think we've reached a convenient time, Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think it will be to everyone's benefit if we break now and resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Mr. Bezruchenko, is it correct that in a number of documents which I think you have reviewed and one or two of which have been admitted in evidence already, there's a reference to an organ or an entity which, in those documents, is referred to as the Operations Control Centre, and I believe in one document it even says "Operational Control Centre of the MOI." Are you aware of those documents -- or any of those documents, I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, there's some problem with the translation, I'm afraid believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Could the witness be assisted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It suddenly switched over to Macedonian. Maybe I should put it off.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I believe it would be number 4, Mr. Bezruchenko, in English.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I'll ask you the question again, Mr. Bezruchenko. Is that correct that in a number of documents which I believe you have reviewed and a number of which were admitted, there are references to a location or a body known as the Operations Control Centre? And I believe that one document refers to even an Operational Control Centre. Are you aware of any such document, Mr. Bezruchenko?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, are you referring to military Macedonian documents or are you referring to police documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I should have specified that the second time I asked the question. I mentioned specifically about the MOI.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Operational Control Centre. There was a headquarters for Operational Action Ramno established in the Ministry of the Interior. Yes, that I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And that headquarter which you are referred to as the Operational Control Centre in Macedonian is known as "DOC"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure if this specific abbreviation implies to DOC.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, would you be familiar with the expression "Dezurni Operativni Centar"?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And this would be the Operational Control Centre which you have referred to; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not necessarily, sir. I believe we should really clarify what this abbreviation means, whether it is "Dezurni Operativna Centra" which literally means "duty officer in the Operational Centre," or whether it means "Dezurni Operativni Centar" which means "Duty Operation Centre." There is some difference here.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: But in terms of substance, Mr. Bezruchenko, is that correct that the duty or responsibility of that body was, in effect, to centralise information which is relevant to the work of the police and, inter alia in criminal cases, to pass that information on to the investigative judge and prosecutor; are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would imagine that this body would have a number of functions. One of those functions would be the nerve centre for collecting all information related to the operational situation in Macedonia, meaning the military situation at the fronts, as well as, perhaps, the operation related to criminal activities. What other functions could be, and I could perhaps give a little bit extended explanation, this may include also the control functions for actual carrying out these operations in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, let me ask two questions, then. Is it correct that this body in fact existed prior to the crisis in 2001; are you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that "dezurni," that is duty officer at the operational centre, probably existed prior this fact, but this is an officer. Not really a body, one officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And when you say in your response that: "This may include also the control functions for actual carrying out these operation in the field," are you stating a belief of yours or are you suggesting that you have material -- or you have reviewed material for the purpose of your report, which indicates that in some instances the Operative Control Centre or Duty Operative Centre, as it should be called, they did so, Mr. Bezruchenko?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would be specifically referring to the headquarters of the Operational Action Ramno.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And is that your evidence, Mr. Bezruchenko, that the headquarter of what you called the Operational Action Ramno was -- or the function of that centre included the control functions for actual carrying out of operations in the field; is that your evidence, Mr. Bezruchenko, or is that an opinion?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that this headquarters definitely had a role in planning and actual carrying out of operations in the field, but I don't really think this was actually limited exclusively to Operational Centre Ramno.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And when you say you believe that the Operational, as you call it, Centre Ramno had a role in planning and actually in carrying out of operation in the field, could you be more precise and indicate what, in your view, allows you to form that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the course of preparation of my report, I came across numerous documents marked "Operation Ramno." Most of these documents are reports from various police bodies and units on the ground to the Operational Centre Ramno. It is pretty obvious in this case that as these reports were actually forwarded to Operational Headquarters Ramno, it was this specific headquarters which was responsible for collecting collecting/analysing these reports, as well as suggesting possible operational response measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And did you see any such documents that would suggest possible operational response measures or did you only see the first type of material which you've indicated, namely, information coming towards the headquarters? In other words, let me ask you perhaps this question: Did you see any order signed by the Operational Centre Ramno, as you call it?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not indicating that Operational Headquarters Ramno was issuing any orders. I only said that it had a role in planning and carrying out such operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Did you see perhaps any plan or map of an operation prepared by the Headquarter Ramno?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see any maps.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And when you say that you saw earlier the possibility that they made possible operation -- or suggestion, it is line 3, suggestion of possible operational response measures, could you tell in what form you suggest those suggestions were being made?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these could be made in the form of verbal suggestions or proposals at briefings and meetings at the Ministry of Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Did you hear or were you present or were you told about any particular instances of such verbal orders being given, and if so, by whom?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: These would be a normal routine procedure in the Ministry of Interior in a situation where a war was going on in the country. I don't really think that the situation warranted any detailed paperwork regarding the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: So the answer to my question is, in fact, that you have not seen any evidence of any such verbal order, but that instead it is a belief that you draw from your experience; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. I did not see any orders specifically coming from the Operational Ramno headquarters, but I have seen lots of reports coming to this --

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Is it also correct -- sorry, did I cut your answer, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Is it also correct that, Mr. Bezruchenko, as you were preparing your amended report and your evidence in this courtroom, you realised that this concept or this doctrine of operational control could come to clash with another aspect of the Prosecution case, or at least what the Prosecution case had evolved to be; is it correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not really. I don't quite understand what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you this, then: Do you recall that during your examination-in-chief, you were being asked a number of questions about disciplinary matters and disciplinary issues by Mr. Saxon? And I refer to the first part of your examination-in-chief on the 4th of October.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No verbal response].

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Bezruchenko, I will ask you again. Do you simply recall being asked a number of questions about disciplinary issues and disciplinary competencies by Mr. Saxon on the 4th of October, 2007?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And do you recall making or giving that particular answer to Mr. Saxon in relation to one of his questions? You said this, and it's the 4th of October of 2007 at page 6070. You said this: "Normally, operational control does not include such issues as discipline and logistics," you said. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And do you agree that this is, in fact, a correct and accurate position under military doctrine, as is evident from the definition of the DOD; do you agree?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And according to that doctrine, and applying again the standard which the DOD, for instance, applied, this would mean that a military officer or a superior who has operational control over a group of men does not have disciplinary or logistical responsibilities in relation to that group; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this is wrong, Mr. Mettraux. I'm afraid we have completely different interpretations of that concept of operational control. We should not mix up two things here. The operational control is operational because it implies operations. Disciplinary control is something else. It implies discipline.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, let me read out to you again the passage from the definition given by the DOD which I read out to you. I'll just read the passage which is relevant here, and it says: "It does not" - that is, operational control - "does not, in and of itself, include authoritative direction for logistics or matters of administration, discipline, internal organisation, or unique training." Do you agree that according to this definition, at least, the concept of operational control does not include discipline or matters of discipline, as it says; do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as defined in this particular document, it is, but this is only part of the answer to the question. The full answer to the question would be that one person, one commander in the field, would normally combine both operational and disciplinary control, so these two types of control are distinctly different.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Is it correct, Mr. Bezruchenko, that this is, in fact, inconsistent, what you just said, inconsistent with the definition of the DOD which I just read out to you?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not. There is no inconsistency here.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Is it also correct, Mr. Bezruchenko, that this new statement that you've made about the combination of operational and disciplinary control is not specifically made in your report; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a very obvious thing, at least to a military expert, Mr. Mettraux, and I don't really think this is something which could be -- I mean, I don't really think this is something which a person could have two opinions about. If a military commander in the field has full responsibility for his troops, he has to have both the operational and disciplinary control. In other words, if I'm a commander of a unit and some man in my unit has committed a breach of discipline, I am the first person up the chain of command to be reported about this to and to take proper measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Are you suggesting that the definition that is given in the lexicon of the DOD is not accurate in terms of military doctrine when it excludes discipline from the realm of operational control?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there is nothing wrong here. I'm saying again, Mr. Mettraux, and perhaps this is some kind of misunderstanding, that you should differentiate between operational control, which is exclusively directed at operations and nothing else, and disciplinary control, which is directed at discipline, and these two types of control are perfectly legitimate to be combined in one commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Isn't it correct --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please make breaks between questions and answers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I apologise to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Isn't that correct that for the first time, Mr. Bezruchenko, in your evidence-in-chief on the 4th of October of 2007, at page 6070, you said this: "These" - and the words should refer to disciplinary powers - "would be granted to the next superior of the commander who would have the operational control of his troops on the ground." Is it what you said?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And does this particular comment appear, as far as you can recall, anywhere in your report?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I don't see any discrepancy here, because what I actually said was that if I commit a disciplinary breach, the next person up the chain of command is supposed to take care about this breach of discipline.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I understand, Mr. Bezruchenko, this is now your evidence here. My question is: Did you mention this particular view of yours or opinion of yours anywhere in your report?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a very clear thing, Mr. Mettraux, and I don't really think that, well, these smallest details would actually be a specific subject of my report. This is simply hair-splitting.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And if I understand your evidence correctly, this particular statement that I've just read to you is not based on the doctrine of operational control; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which specific statement do you mean, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I will read it out to you again, Mr. Bezruchenko. It's from the 4th of October of 2007. It's page 6070, and it reads like that. It says: "These powers," and you are referring at this stage to these disciplinary powers, "would be granted to the next superior of the commander who would have the operational control of his troops on the ground."

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I could specify your question, Mr. Mettraux, disciplinary powers in relation to what?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Bezruchenko, I'm asking you about the answer that you gave to Mr. Saxon, to his particular question, and perhaps if I can assist you, I can read the question that was put to you. It's again the same page, Mr. Bezruchenko. It reads this: "How does this paragraph" - that's paragraph 415 of your statement - "relate to -- actually, let me step back a little bit. There's a term that I'd like to ask you, if you can define a term for me, please. The term is 'operational control'." That's your response: "Well, according to the concept of operational control, a commander who is responsible to carry out a certain mission must exercise his authority to organise, deploy and direct his forces in operational sense, that is, to make sure that his mission is accomplished." And then you added: "Normally, operational control does not include such issues as discipline, logistics and -- logistics." And then Mr. Saxon asked you this: "And when you say, 'Normally operational control does not include such issues as discipline, logistics and -- logistics,' for example, the aspect of discipline, who would be expected, if not the commander, to exercise operational control with respect to discipline?" And your answer was this: "That would be -- these powers would be granted to the next superior of the commander, who would have the operational control of his troops on the ground." Do you recall that exchange?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And in answer to my question, did you make that particular point which you made to Mr. Saxon in response to his question anywhere in your report?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, as is clear from this exchange, I provided an accurate description of the operational control. And regarding the second part of this exchange, the control of disciplinary powers or, in fact, the disciplinary control belongs to the same person who is exercising operational control of his particular unit. But if it is found that a commander of this particular unit is committing some breaches of discipline, it is next up the chain of command who is to take care of that. It's as simple as that.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, I have two questions to follow up on this. You first said that, yes, you have made that point in your report. Would you remember where, generally in your report, that evidence or that opinion would be given?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir. Which specific point you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I'm referring in particular to the suggestion that disciplinary powers would be granted to the next superior of the commander who would have the operational control of his troops on the ground.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: My report was based on documents, sir, and I would like you to please indicate to me which specific document you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I think we're talking at cross-purpose, Mr. Bezruchenko. I understood that your evidence here is that this particular point which you are now making to the effect that the disciplinary powers would be granted to the next superior of the commander who would have the operational control of his troops on the ground, is to be found somewhere in your report, and my first question was: Could you indicate if, indeed, this is to be found in your report, and if so, in what part of that report, if you can recall?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Mettraux, I don't quite understand what you mean by "operational powers" in relation to discipline. There is, in my understanding, no such thing as operational powers in relation to discipline. There are operational power -- I mean operational control and there are disciplinary powers. Well, regarding the specific point which you're referring to, the point of disciplinary control was reflected in my report -- in the part of my report, I mean, which speaks about the Law of Internal Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: So it is your evidence here, sir, that this particular point, and I use the expression "powers" because it is the one you used in your evidence-in-chief yourself, your evidence is that, in fact, that particular point about these disciplinary powers granted to the next superior of the commander, who would have the operational control of his troops on the ground, is in fact, in your -- in the part of your report that discusses the MOI; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is correct, sir, is that my report contains a portion on the disciplinary powers of the head of the Ministry of Interior, as reflected in the Law on Internal Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And simply, Mr. Bezruchenko, I don't want to muddy the water, but for the sake of clarity, this particular statement that I've read to you a number of times, is it a statement which you recall as having been made somewhere in your report?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't quite understand what you mean, sir. Which statement do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. Bezruchenko, for not being clear. Your statement made at page 6070 to the effect that disciplinary powers, your terms, would be granted to the next superior of the commander who would have the operational control of his troops on the ground, is it, as far as you can recollect, a statement or a finding or an opinion which you gave somewhere in your report?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we are referring to specific wording of what you call "statement," well, I don't think I have this wording in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And simply to clarify the second matter for the record and to be sure that we understand each other, Mr. Bezruchenko, I would like to be clear on the issue of the scope, if you wish, of the concept of operational control. Is your evidence now that the concept of operational control does, in fact, include the concept of -- or does include disciplinary powers?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, this is a wrong statement. As I mentioned previously, and I repeat it again, there is operational control and there are disciplinary powers, and there is no way of mixing these two up.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And when the DOD says that operational control does not, in and of itself, include disciplinary powers or matters of discipline, are you taking issue with that proposal?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: This proposal, as formulated in the DOD document, is absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And I believe that later in your evidence, sorry, you said to Mr. Saxon, and again correct me if it's a poor summary, that in a normal military structure superiors have disciplinary powers over their subordinates. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And just as a matter of clarity, did you discuss at all the issue of disciplinary powers in the context of the Ministry of Defence or the army in your report?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Is that correct that you did not deal with any disciplinary powers or any disciplinary competencies as might have the commander-in-chief of the army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my report, I was, among other things, describing the legislation pertaining to the organisation of the defence of the country, including the Law on Defence, and I think I provided maybe a, maybe a little bit brief, a succinct description of the law and the basic clauses it addresses, but I don't think that I made a specific point about disciplinary powers in the military, which again are pretty obvious things and I don't really think need any special attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: But you do pay attention in your report to the issue of disciplinary powers in the Ministry of the Interior, as you say it; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, because the law deals with this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And so does the law applicable to the army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not entirely certain which particular clause deals with this issue, but army is an army, and disciplinary matters in the army are pretty obvious to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Just going back to your report for a moment, Mr. Bezruchenko, is it correct that in your report, you make the suggestions that Mr. Boskoski, and I think I have read that passage to you already, had operational control over -- of police forces; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And is that correct that in your report, you also suggest that Minister Boskoski had certain disciplinary responsibilities vis-a-vis those forces; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I will come back in a moment, Mr. Bezruchenko, to the issue of disciplinary competencies and powers, as you see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: If Mr. Bezruchenko would please be shown his report once again. I believe this is Exhibit P466. And if the Registry could please turn to page 107.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Mr. Bezruchenko, this should be the same page I believe you still have in front of you. This is the subsection of your report 3.3.3.1 dealing with operational control.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And I would like to turn your attention once again, on the same paragraph, that's paragraph 371. That's the paragraph in your report where you suggest that Minister Boskoski exercise operational control of police forces, and you add that this operational control was manifested in orders to deploy police at various crisis areas. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And is that correct that for the -- for your conclusion, if you so wish, to be correct in this matter, it would have to be accepted first -- I will simply list them for you, and you will tell me whether you agree with them -- for your conclusions and approach to be accepted by this Chamber, it would have to be accepted first that this military doctrine of operational control is acceptable or is applicable, I'm sorry, in the context of a military and civilian structure; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't quite understand your question, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, let me put it slightly better. Do you agree that the doctrine of operational control is a military doctrine?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As expressed in the document which I used, yes, it is basically a military doctrine.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And you will agree then, Mr. Bezruchenko, that for it to apply to the Ministry of Interior of the Republic of Macedonia in this case, it would have to be accepted by the Trial Chamber that this military doctrine can apply, in fact, to a civilian context; do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: This may be an issue, and maybe not. In fact, if we come back to the document which you have just shown to me, Mr. Mettraux, which is "Pravilnik Za Vrsenje Na Rabotite," it clearly speaks, even in the English translation, of an operational control. Well, so basically we are back to the square 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, if you can simply respond to the question, Mr. Bezruchenko. Do you agree that in order to accept your conclusions and your findings on that point as regard operational control, it would have to be accepted that this particular military doctrine would apply in the context of a civilian structure, such as the Ministry of Interior of the Republic of Macedonia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer to this would be the following, Mr. Mettraux: The forces of the Ministry of Interior were a component of the security forces of the Republic of Macedonia and were deployed in combat operations on the ground. Therefore, the concept of the operational control, as you define it in its military application, would certainly be applicable to the units of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
