utterances.text: So if I understand your response correctly, Mr. Bezruchenko, your suggestion is that, yes, this doctrine -- military doctrine of operational control applies or can apply to a civilian structure, and it does apply, in your view, to the situation of the Ministry of Interior of the Republic of Macedonia. Is that a correct summary?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am specifically referring to the forces or, rather, units of special police of the Ministry of Interior. I don't know to which extent they could be described as civilian structures.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Is your evidence then, Mr. Bezruchenko, somewhat qualified to the effect that only those units, you mentioned the special police, for instance, which took part in what you called "forces," "use of force," I don't know what expression you wanted to use, would come under the application of that doctrine, or would your application of that doctrine be broader in scope?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may refer you to the book which was written by prominent military experts, "The War in Macedonia," which clearly speaks about the security forces of Macedonia being made of two components; the Ministry of Interior, as such, as an institution, and the Armed Forces of the Republic of Macedonia, so according to the opinion of these experts, and I tend to concur with them, the concept of operational control, in its military sense, will be equally applicable to the entirety of the entity which is called the security forces of Macedonia, being - excuse me, sir - being made up of forces of the Ministry of Interior and the Ministry of Interior itself, as well as the Army of the Republic of Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I'm grateful for this, Mr. Bezruchenko. Perhaps I should ask you this: Are you aware of any precedent or are you aware of any authority in your field or in others which would suggest that, in fact, this military doctrine could possibly apply to a civilian organ or a civilian institution; are you aware of any such precedent or authority?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: We may go back to the Law on Defence of the Republic of Macedonia, which clearly speaks of a possibility of involvement of the Ministry of Interior in military operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: But you do agree, Mr. Bezruchenko, that the Law on Defence does not speak of operational control as regard the Ministry of Interior and its forces; do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Is it also correct that for the Chamber to accept your conclusion on that point, it would have to accept that Mr. Boskoski in fact had such so-called operational control; do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't quite understand your question, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, do you agree that your report -- I could put it better to you, Mr. Bezruchenko. Your report suggests and you're inviting the Chamber to accept two things: That not only did the theory of operational control apply to the Ministry of Interior in Macedonia at the relevant time, but in particular to the minister himself, Mr. Boskoski, and that in this particular instance you say he had that control; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think, just for the record perhaps, I may say again that in the war situation which was taking place in Macedonia in 2001, the concept of operational control de facto applied both -- to both components of the Macedonian security forces, these being the Ministry of the Interior and the Army of the Republic of Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Is that also correct, Mr. Bezruchenko, that what you are inviting, in effect, the Chamber to do is to apply this doctrine of operational control to some extent, but not to its full extent, to Mr. Boskoski; is that correct, that's in effect what you're asking the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not, sir. There are no implications attached to my statement. What I said is purely based on my professional experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Isn't it correct, Mr. Bezruchenko, that in effect what you're asking the Chamber to do is to apply this theory of operational control, as far as you say is relevant to demonstrating authority on the part of the minister over police forces, but to refrain from applying that doctrine to its end when it relates to disciplinary matters? Would that be a fair summary?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid not, sir. I'm afraid I am repeating this again. We do not really have to mix up two things, operational control and disciplinary powers. These are absolutely different things. But that does not necessarily mean that they can be combined in the authority of one person. This is what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Would that be a convenient time, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. We adjourn now for the weekend. We resume at 2.15 on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 22nd day of October, 2007, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.45 p.m.,
